q: A patient with a ruptured AAA is conscious with a systolic BP of 80 mmHg. What is the resuscitation target before the aorta is clamped?
o: Permissive hypotension: a talking patient with systolic around 70–90
why: Permissive hypotension limits bleeding until the clamp is on; activate major haemorrhage and have blood running before induction.

q: When should anaesthesia be induced for open repair of a ruptured AAA?
o: In the anaesthetic room, before transfer
On the table, with the patient prepared and draped and the surgeon scrubbed
After an arterial line, CVC and epidural are placed
why: Induction can cause catastrophic collapse: loss of abdominal muscle tone releases the tamponade and PPV reduces preload. Induce only when the surgeon is ready to clamp.

q: What are the effects of aortic cross-clamping?
o: Proximal hypertension (raised afterload) and distal ischaemic vasodilatation
Increased renal blood flow below the clamp
why: Afterload rises above the clamp (risking MI and arrhythmia); manage by deepening anaesthesia or GTN. Below the clamp, ischaemia causes vasodilatation.

q: What happens when the aortic cross-clamp is released?
o: Sudden fall in afterload with hypotension, acidosis and hyperkalaemia
why: Reperfusion of the ischaemic bed lowers SVR and releases lactate and potassium; give vasopressors and ask the surgeon to release each limb slowly.

q: After repair of a ruptured AAA, a ventilated patient becomes oliguric with rising airway pressures and a tense abdomen. Bladder pressure is 25 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
why: Abdominal compartment syndrome is pressure over 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (intra-abdominal hypertension is over 12 mmHg). It follows massive resuscitation and retroperitoneal haematoma.

q: After thoracoabdominal aneurysm repair, a patient has paraplegia with loss of pain and temperature but preserved vibration and proprioception. What has happened?
o: Anterior spinal cord syndrome from loss of the artery of Adamkiewicz
why: Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares the dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception).

q: What is the in-hospital mortality of ruptured AAA?
why: In-hospital mortality is around 40%; overall mortality including pre-hospital deaths is around 80%.

q: Which Stanford type of aortic dissection is a surgical emergency?
o: Type A: any involvement of the ascending aorta
Type B: distal to the left subclavian
why: Stanford A involves the ascending aorta and needs emergency surgery; type B is generally managed medically with BP and heart rate control unless complicated.

q: What is the "lethal triad" in massive haemorrhage?
why: Coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia worsen each other; warm everything and correct them early.

q: Which complication of massive transfusion is caused by citrate in blood products?
why: Citrate binds calcium, causing hypocalcaemia and myocardial depression; give calcium.
